problem: The sentence is garbled: 'If Z  1, φ > 1.' The comparison operator is missing, so the student sees an incomplete condition and cannot tell which case gives φ above 1 and which gives φ below 1.
fix: State both cases: 'If Z > 1, (Z − 1)/P is positive, so ln φ > 0 and φ > 1. If Z < 1, ln φ < 0 and φ < 1.'

where: Section 2, paragraph after the ln φ formula
problem: The integrand (Z − 1)/P does not vanish as P → 0. Since Z − 1 ≈ BP/RT at low pressure, (Z − 1)/P tends to the finite value B/RT. The integral converges because that limit is finite, not because it is zero. As written, a student will believe the integrand goes to zero at the lower limit.
fix: Say: 'As P → 0, Z → 1 and (Z − 1)/P tends to a finite limit, B/RT. The integrand has no singularity there, which is why the lower limit can be taken as zero even though P appears in the denominator.'

problem: 'Reliable for non-polar gases up to a few bar' states the validity in absolute pressure. The virial correlation is limited by reduced pressure (roughly Pr below about 0.5) and by Tr above about 0.8. For a gas with a high critical pressure, 'a few bar' is far too cautious and misleads the student about when the formula can be used.
fix: Say: 'It is reliable for non-polar gases at low reduced pressure, roughly Pr < 0.5, and for Tr above about 0.8.'

where: Section 1, sentence after the φ formula
problem: 'Some syllabi call φ the fugacity coefficient and write it as f/p' is confusing: the chapter has just defined φ as the fugacity coefficient, so it reads as if the name were a syllabus variant. The point is only the alternative symbol f/p.
fix: Say: 'Some books write the fugacity coefficient as f/p instead of φ.'
